summary:
Christianity emerged within Jewish history and spread through a Mediterranean world profoundly shaped by Greek language, education, and political experience. Understanding that environment helps us see both the opportunities and the conflicts early Christians encountered. It does not reduce Christian origins to a single cultural influence.

Classical Greece consisted of distinct city-states, or poleis. Athens was influential, but its democratic institutions were neither universal across Greece nor inclusive by modern standards. Greek intellectual life was equally varied: poets, public speakers, philosophers, and worshipers offered different accounts of the good life and humanity’s relation to the divine.

Alexander’s conquests and the kingdoms that followed widened the reach of Greek culture. This Hellenistic world involved cultural exchange and local adaptation as well as conquest. Greek language and learning continued to matter under Roman political rule. Political control and cultural influence therefore need to be tracked separately.

For biblical study, the crucial question is how communities used shared cultural forms while making distinctive claims. Acts 17 offers one literary portrayal of that encounter: Paul’s speech engages an Athenian setting, yet the resurrection provokes disagreement. Read such texts with attention to their authors’ purposes, rather than treating them as unmediated recordings. As you watch, distinguish historical background, Reeves’s interpretation, and your own theological conclusions.

keyIdeas.title: A world of cities
keyIdeas.explanation: The polis joined civic institutions, law, communal identity, and religious life. City-states had different constitutions; “Greek” did not imply a unified nation-state.

keyIdeas.title: Participation had boundaries
keyIdeas.explanation: Athenian democracy gave citizens a direct political role while excluding women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners from that citizenship. Ask who belonged whenever a source celebrates freedom.

keyIdeas.title: Conquest reshaped cultural contact
keyIdeas.explanation: Alexander’s campaigns and successor kingdoms extended Greek influence. Hellenization was uneven: local traditions persisted and interacted with new institutions.

keyIdeas.title: Rome did not erase Greece
keyIdeas.explanation: Greek culture retained prestige under Roman rule. A community could live under Roman imperial authority while using Greek language and educational traditions.

keyIdeas.title: Shared language, disputed meaning
keyIdeas.explanation: Communication across cultures requires familiar terms, but a familiar term need not carry an identical worldview. In Acts 17, engagement with Greek hearers does not eliminate disagreement over resurrection.

keyIdeas.title: Sources are arguments too
keyIdeas.explanation: Plato’s presentation of Socrates and Acts’ presentation of Paul have literary purposes. Identify genre, narrator, audience, and claims before drawing historical conclusions.

terms.definition: A Greek city-state / city-states, understood as a political community as well as a place.
Conventionally, the era after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE through the rise of Roman domination; also the Greek-influenced cultures of that era.
Processes by which Greek cultural practices spread and were adapted, resisted, or combined with local traditions.
The broadly shared form of Greek used across much of the eastern Mediterranean in the Hellenistic and Roman periods, including the New Testament.
Evidence from the period or historical process being investigated; proximity does not make a source neutral or infallible.

mastery.question: Why is “ancient Greece was a democracy” a misleading generalization?
mastery.answer: It treats one political form, especially associated with Athens, as universal. Many poleis had other constitutions, and even Athenian political participation excluded much of the population.

mastery.question: Distinguish Greek cultural influence from Greek political sovereignty.
mastery.answer: Language, education, art, and intellectual traditions can persist after political power changes hands. Roman conquest did not end the prestige or use of Greek culture.

mastery.question: What would count as evidence of Hellenization, and what would not?
mastery.answer: Greek inscriptions, educational institutions, artistic forms, or adapted civic practices can provide evidence. A Greek name alone does not establish total replacement of a community’s earlier identity or beliefs.

mastery.question: How does Acts 17 portray both connection and conflict?
mastery.answer: The speech engages an Athenian religious setting and quotes poetry, yet its proclamation of judgment and resurrection produces mixed responses. Cultural intelligibility is not the same as doctrinal agreement.

mastery.question: Why read Plato’s Apology critically even though it is a primary source?
mastery.answer: It is Plato’s literary presentation of Socrates’ defense, not a modern verbatim recording. Its philosophical and rhetorical purposes shape what it can establish.

mastery.question: How can Greek background illuminate Christianity without erasing its Jewish matrix?
mastery.answer: Study the languages and institutions through which Christians communicated alongside their engagement with Jewish scriptures, practices, and messianic expectations. Influence is multidirectional and does not by itself establish derivation.

reflection: Which exclusions become visible when you look at a celebrated institution from the perspective of people denied membership? How might this change your reading of church history?
Where does your understanding of Christianity rely on the vocabulary of your own culture? Which terms communicate faithfully, and which quietly reshape the message?
Read Acts 17 together. Where do you each see patient engagement, and where do you see a boundary that remains unresolved?
What evidence would make you revise a familiar story about the relationship between faith and philosophy? Name one claim you want to investigate rather than inherit.

quiz.question: Which description best fits the classical Greek polis?
options: A political community with its own institutions
A province administered by a Roman governor
A federation joining all Greek-speaking people
A philosophical school devoted to public speaking
quiz.explanation: The polis was a city-state and civic community. Shared language or religious traditions did not make all poleis a single state.

quiz.question: What is the main problem with treating Athens as representative of every Greek city?
options: Athens had no political institutions
Greek city-states had varied constitutions and histories
Athens did not use Greek
Greek cities were always ruled by Persia
quiz.explanation: Athens is unusually prominent in surviving evidence. Its prominence should not turn its institutions into a universal Greek pattern.

quiz.question: Which statement best qualifies Athenian democracy?
options: Its assembly included every adult resident
It required representative parliamentary elections
Citizen participation coexisted with major exclusions
It abolished slavery as a condition of citizenship
quiz.explanation: Direct participation by citizens did not amount to universal inclusion. Women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners were excluded from political citizenship.

quiz.question: Which event conventionally marks the beginning of the Hellenistic period?
options: The founding of Rome
The birth of Jesus
The destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE
Alexander’s death in 323 BCE
quiz.explanation: Alexander’s death is the conventional period boundary. His earlier conquests helped create the conditions for the successor kingdoms and wider cultural exchange.

quiz.question: An inscription combines a local deity’s name with Greek wording. What is the most responsible initial inference?
options: Greek linguistic influence interacted with local religious practice
The entire population abandoned its earlier religion
The city must have been governed directly from Athens
The inscription proves the arrival of Christianity
quiz.explanation: The evidence supports interaction at the level the inscription reveals. It does not establish wholesale cultural replacement or identify every resident’s beliefs.

quiz.question: Why does Greek background remain relevant after Roman conquest?
options: Rome prohibited its own language throughout the empire
Cultural practices can persist under a new political authority
Roman government restored every Greek city’s independence
Christian authors all wrote before Roman expansion
quiz.explanation: Political and cultural histories do not share identical boundaries. Greek language and education remained important in the Roman world.

quiz.question: What does the term Koine identify in biblical studies?
options: A single Greek philosophical school
The constitution of the Athenian assembly
A widely shared form of Greek used in the New Testament
A Roman law establishing religious toleration
quiz.explanation: Koine refers to a common form of Greek, not a particular school or law. Its widespread use helps explain communication across different communities.

quiz.question: In Acts 17, why is agreement on some cultural references insufficient to establish agreement with Paul?
options: The speech contains no recognizable cultural references
All hearers are portrayed as accepting the message
Greek was unknown in Athens
The proclamation of resurrection elicits conflicting responses
quiz.explanation: Acts portrays mixed responses to resurrection. Shared language and points of contact make debate possible without guaranteeing assent.

quiz.question: How should Plato’s Apology be used as historical evidence?
options: As a literary presentation whose purposes must be evaluated
As an audio transcript preserved without editorial shaping
As evidence that all Greeks shared Socrates’ views
As a Christian account written by Paul
quiz.explanation: A primary source remains a constructed work. Its author, genre, and aims are part of the evidence, rather than obstacles that can simply be ignored.

quiz.question: Which comparison most carefully relates Christianity to its Greek environment?
options: Greek influence proves that Christianity had no Jewish roots
Greek forms of communication interacted with Jewish scriptures and distinctive Christian claims
Shared vocabulary guarantees identical meanings
Cultural background alone settles whether a theological claim is true
quiz.explanation: This account allows multiple historical relationships. Showing that a community uses a language or concept does not, by itself, settle its origins or the truth of its beliefs.

quiz.question: A historian finds Greek-style artwork in a city. Which follow-up would best test how deeply Greek practices shaped local life?
options: Assume every resident held the same worldview
Ignore local evidence because artistic style is decisive
Compare inscriptions, institutions, household evidence, and local traditions
Date the city solely from a modern photograph
quiz.explanation: Different kinds of evidence can show whether influence was broad, selective, elite, or adapted. One artifact rarely supports a total claim about a society.

quiz.question: Which note best separates observation from interpretation while watching this lecture?
options: “Everything the lecturer says is equally certain.”
“The title proves which interpretation is correct.”
“Historical context can be ignored when discussing theology.”
“Here is the source cited; here is the lecturer’s inference; here is my question about it.”
quiz.explanation: Separating evidence, inference, and response makes disagreement more precise. It also helps you identify which claims need further investigation.
